The text studies a directed graph (or relation) \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) that is both reflexive and point-symmetric. Reflexivity means that every vertex has a loop, so \(v\in \Gamma(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). Point-symmetry means that the automorphism group of \(\Gamma\) acts transitively on the vertex set: any vertex can be mapped to any other vertex by an automorphism of the relation. In particular, all vertices have the same local structure. The discussion focuses on a vertex \(v\in V\) whose out-neighborhood \(\Gamma(v)\) is finite.

For a nonnegative integer \(j\), \(\Gamma^j(v)\) denotes the set of vertices that can be reached from \(v\) by a directed path of length at most, or exactly depending on the convention used in the relation composition, \(j\) steps under repeated application of \(\Gamma\). Similarly, \(\Gamma^{-}(v)\) denotes the in-neighborhood of \(v\), that is, the set of vertices \(u\) such that \(v\in \Gamma(u)\). The key assumption is that, for some integer \(j\in\mathbb N\),

\[
\Gamma^j(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\}.
\]

This condition says that among all vertices reachable from \(v\) in \(j\) steps, the only one that has an edge back to \(v\) is \(v\) itself. In other words, there is no nontrivial return to \(v\) within this range.

Under these hypotheses, the main result establishes the growth inequality

\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1.
\]

This means that, as one passes from the \((j-1)\)-st neighborhood of \(v\) to the \(j\)-th neighborhood, the number of reachable vertices increases by at least \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\). The subtraction of \(1\) accounts for the reflexive loop at \(v\), since \(v\) is already present in the previous neighborhood.

By iterating this inequality, one obtains the linear lower bound

\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr)j.
\]

Indeed, starting from \(|\Gamma^0(v)|=1\), each successive neighborhood must contribute at least \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\) new vertices, as long as the required non-return condition is satisfied. Thus the size of the iterated out-neighborhood grows at least linearly with \(j\).

This result has several important consequences. First, it confirms Seymour’s conjecture in the case of vertex-symmetric graphs. Seymour’s conjecture concerns the existence of vertices whose higher-order neighborhoods grow in a prescribed way, and the theorem gives exactly the required expansion estimate in the symmetric setting.

Second, the theorem supports the Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture for vertex-symmetric graphs. That conjecture relates the minimum out-degree of a directed graph to the existence of short directed cycles. The growth bound implies that if no short cycle returns to \(v\), then the reachable sets from \(v\) must expand rapidly. In a finite graph, such expansion cannot continue indefinitely, forcing the existence of a short directed cycle.

Finally, the result generalizes an earlier theorem of Shepherdson. Shepherdson’s result applied to more restricted algebraic or graph-theoretic settings, while the present theorem applies to the broader class of point-symmetric reflexive relations with finite out-neighborhoods. Thus the text provides a unified and more general expansion principle for symmetric directed graphs and relations.

This text investigates the growth of iterated neighborhoods in directed graphs, or more generally in reflexive relations, under strong symmetry assumptions. The setting is a point-symmetric, or vertex-transitive, reflexive relation \(\Gamma\), meaning that every vertex has a loop and that the automorphism group acts transitively on the set of vertices. In addition, the relation is assumed to have finite neighborhoods, so that for each vertex \(v\), the set of out-neighbors \(\Gamma(v)\) is finite.

The central question is how large the \(j\)-th iterated neighborhood \(\Gamma^j(v)\) must be when no directed cycle of length at most \(j\) returns to \(v\). This condition is expressed as

\[
\Gamma^j(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\},
\]

where \(\Gamma^{-}(v)\) denotes the set of in-neighbors of \(v\). Intuitively, this hypothesis says that, apart from the trivial loop at \(v\), none of the vertices reachable from \(v\) in \(j\) steps sends an edge back to \(v\). Thus the graph has no short directed return to \(v\) within the range being considered.

The main theorem proves that, under these assumptions, the iterated neighborhoods must grow by at least \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\) at each step. More precisely, for every positive integer \(j\) satisfying the above non-return condition, one has

\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1.
\]

This inequality shows that each new layer of reachable vertices contributes at least as much growth as the initial out-neighborhood, except for the unavoidable overlap at the base vertex caused by reflexivity.

By iterating the inequality, one obtains the linear lower bound

\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr)j.
\]

Thus, in a vertex-symmetric reflexive graph, the size of the set of vertices reachable from \(v\) in at most \(j\) steps grows at least linearly with \(j\), with slope \(|\Gamma(v)|-1\). This is the natural directed analogue of additive growth phenomena in groups and highly symmetric graphs.

The proof relies on the symmetry of the relation. Since the automorphism group acts transitively on vertices, local properties around one vertex can be transferred to any other vertex. This makes it possible to compare neighborhoods and derive uniform expansion estimates. The reflexive assumption ensures that the sequence

\[
\{v\}\subseteq \Gamma(v)\subseteq \Gamma^2(v)\subseteq \cdots
\]

is increasing, so that growth can be measured by the number of genuinely new vertices appearing at each step.

The result has several important consequences. First, it confirms Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture in the case of vertex-symmetric graphs. Seymour’s conjecture predicts, in one formulation, that in every finite directed graph without loops, some vertex has at least as many second out-neighbors as first out-neighbors. The theorem gives a stronger structural statement for the symmetric case, because it provides a lower bound for all iterated neighborhoods as long as short returns are absent.

Second, the theorem supports the Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture in the vertex-symmetric setting. That conjecture asserts that every finite directed graph with minimum out-degree \(d\) contains a directed cycle of length at most \(\lceil n/d\rceil\), where \(n\) is the number of vertices. The linear growth estimate implies that if no short directed cycle exists, then the reachable sets must grow too large, eventually exceeding the total number of vertices. This forces the existence of a directed cycle of the predicted length in the symmetric case.

Finally, the theorem generalizes an additive result of Shepherdson. Shepherdson’s theorem concerns growth in groups and shows that, under suitable conditions, repeated products of a set expand at least linearly. The present result extends this additive principle from group multiplication to the broader framework of point-symmetric reflexive relations. In this way, it connects additive combinatorics, graph theory, and the study of highly symmetric directed structures.

Overall, the text establishes a clear and powerful growth principle: in a finite-neighborhood, point-symmetric, reflexive relation, the absence of short returns forces linear expansion of iterated neighborhoods. This principle not only unifies earlier additive results but also yields significant applications to major conjectures about directed cycles and neighborhood growth.

We prove a growth theorem for point-symmetric reflexive relations.  Let \(\Gamma\) be a locally finite reflexive relation whose automorphism group is transitive on \(V\).  For \(v\in V\) and \(j\ge 1\), if
\[
\Gamma^{j}(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\},
\]
then
\[
|\Gamma^{j}(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1 .
\]
In particular, iterated out-neighborhoods grow at least linearly until they meet the in-neighborhood of the starting point.  The proof uses isoperimetric methods for relations and yields a unified formulation for several classical expansion phenomena.  As consequences, we recover and extend results connected with Seymour’s second neighborhood conjecture for symmetric settings, the vertex-transitive case of the Caccetta–Häggkvist girth bound, and Shepherdson-type additive inequalities.

Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a directed graph (relation), typically assumed **reflexive** \((v,v)\in E\), **vertex-transitive**, and **locally finite** in the sense that every out-neighborhood \(\Gamma(v)\) is finite. For \(j\ge 0\), write

\[
\Gamma^0(v)=\{v\},\qquad 
\Gamma^j(v)=\Gamma(\Gamma^{j-1}(v))
\]

for the set of vertices reachable from \(v\) by a directed walk of length at most/ exactly according to the reflexive convention; in the reflexive setting these sets are increasing.

## Main theorem

The central result is a growth theorem for powers of a vertex-transitive directed graph:

\[
\boxed{
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1
}
\]

provided that

\[
\Gamma^j(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\},
\]

where \(\Gamma^{-}(v)\) is the in-neighborhood of \(v\).

Equivalently: as long as the \(j\)-th layer reachable from \(v\) has not “wrapped around” to an in-neighbor of \(v\) other than \(v\) itself, the reachable set must grow by at least

\[
|\Gamma(v)|-1
\]

new vertices at each step.

If the graph is not taken to be reflexive and the ordinary out-degree is \(d\), then after adjoining loops one has \(|\Gamma(v)|=d+1\), so the bound becomes

\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+d.
\]

## Iterated form

Applying the theorem repeatedly gives

\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|
\ge 1+j\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr)
\]

as long as the no-return condition

\[
\Gamma^i(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\}
\]

holds for \(1\le i\le j\).

Thus vertex-transitivity forces linear expansion of reachable sets until a directed cycle returning toward \(v\) appears.

## Consequence for directed cycles / girth

Let \(\Gamma\) be finite, vertex-transitive, with

\[
|V|=n,\qquad |\Gamma(v)|=r
\]

in the reflexive convention. If no short directed cycle through \(v\) exists, then the sets \(\Gamma^j(v)\) must keep expanding. Since they cannot exceed \(n\), the inequality

\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+j(r-1)
\]

implies that a return must occur once

\[
1+j(r-1)>n.
\]

Hence the directed girth \(g\) satisfies a Caccetta–Häggkvist-type bound

\[
g\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{r-1}\right\rceil
\]

or, in the non-reflexive convention with out-degree \(d=r-1\),

\[
\boxed{
g\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{d}\right\rceil .
}
\]

So every finite vertex-transitive digraph of out-degree \(d\) contains a directed cycle of length at most \(\lceil n/d\rceil\).

## Additive-combinatorial interpretation

When the digraph is a Cayley digraph of a group \(G\), with

\[
\Gamma(x)=xB
\]

for some finite generating set \(B\subseteq G\) containing the identity, the theorem becomes a product-set growth statement:

\[
|B^j|\ge |B^{j-1}|+|B|-1
\]

under the corresponding non-periodicity/no-return condition. This generalizes classical additive results such as the Moser–Scherck–Kemperman–Wehn type inequalities.

## Summary

The article’s main message is that **local finiteness plus vertex-transitivity imposes unavoidable expansion** in directed graphs. Before a reachable set can return to an in-neighbor of the starting vertex, it must satisfy

\[
\boxed{
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1.
}
\]

This yields:

1. linear lower bounds  
   \[
   |\Gamma^j(v)|\ge 1+j(|\Gamma(v)|-1);
   \]

2. short directed cycle bounds in finite vertex-transitive digraphs; in particular  
   \[
   g\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{d}\right\rceil;
   \]

3. product-set growth inequalities for Cayley graphs and group subsets;

4. a vertex-transitive confirmation of the expected Caccetta–Häggkvist behavior.

A typical formulation is:

> where \(N^{+}(v)\) is the out-neighborhood of \(v\) and \(N^{++}(v)\) is the set of vertices reachable from \(v\) by a directed path of length two.

under the appropriate no-2-cycle condition.

**Abstract.**  
We study the growth of iterated neighborhoods in point-symmetric graphs, i.e. graphs whose automorphism group acts transitively on vertices. Under the finite-degree assumption, so that each neighborhood \(\Gamma(v)\) is finite, one obtains a uniform expansion bound for successive powers of the neighborhood operator. The key inequality states that, for a vertex \(v\) and an integer \(j\ge 1\), under the usual non-return condition  
\[
\Gamma^j(v)\cap \Gamma^{-}(v)=\{v\},
\]
the \(j\)-th neighborhood satisfies  
\[
|\Gamma^j(v)|\ge |\Gamma^{j-1}(v)|+|\Gamma(v)|-1 .
\]
Iterating this estimate gives the linear growth corollary  
\[
|\Gamma^j(v)| \ge 1+\bigl(|\Gamma(v)|-1\bigr)j .
\]
Thus, in a finite-degree point-symmetric graph, iterated neighborhoods cannot grow too slowly before encountering a backward neighbor of the base vertex. This graph-theoretic expansion principle parallels classical additive-combinatorial results of Shepherdson on growth of iterated sumsets/products, where sets with no short additive return satisfy lower bounds of the form \(|jB|\ge 1+j(|B|-1)\). The neighborhood formulation may be viewed as a vertex-transitive graph analogue of these additive growth estimates.
